title: The receivable that never arrives
question: Where an organization books large sums as owed to it, do those sums get collected, keep growing, or vanish from the balance sheet without a trace?
finding: Among 477 organizations with full returns, there are 41 years in which a balance of $250,000 or more owed to the organization (and at least 15% of the year's revenue) fell by three-quarters or more. In 15 of them cash and investments rose to match, so the money appears to have been collected; in 2 net assets fell with no line explaining it, the largest being St James Infirmary, where $6.5 million owed at the start of the year ended 30 June 2024 was $1,185 at the end; the other 24 were set against debts, absorbed by a deficit, or cannot be traced from the return. Separately, 9 organizations show a balance that has risen at each of the last four year-ends or more and faster than revenue, $28.4 million in all, led by Horizon Services, Inc with $7.7 million, 36% of a year's revenue.
how: Money owed is pledges and grants receivable plus accounts receivable on the balance sheet of each full return (Part X lines 3 and 4). "Disappeared" is an opening balance of $250,000 or more, and 15% or more of that year's revenue, that ends the year at a quarter of that or less. Where it went is read from the same return: a rise in cash and investments of at least half the fall means collected; a fall in liabilities of that size means set against debts; a deficit of that size means written off or spent; a fall in net assets that the return does not explain (from the roll-forward screen) means no entry. "Grows every year" is four or more consecutive year-ends each higher than the last, ending at the latest return, a closing balance of $500,000 or more and a quarter of revenue, and a balance that has grown at least half as fast again as revenue. Ordered: no entry, then deficit or unclear, then debts, then collected, then growing balances.
limits: A large receivable is ordinary for an organization paid in arrears by government, and a growing one may mean only that a funder is paying more slowly. A multi-year pledge is booked in full when promised and then runs down for years with no new revenue, which is correct accounting. A receivable that is written off should appear as a bad-debt expense, and one returned to a funder as a reduction of revenue; where neither appears the return, not necessarily the organization, is at fault. Only the aged list of who owes what, in the audited statements, settles it. A pattern here is a reason to ask for the audited statements, not a finding.
